abstract: I develop a new method for estimating production functions with labor‐augmenting technology and apply it to markup estimation. The method imposes limited parametric restrictions and generalizes prior approaches that rely on the CES production function. I first extend the canonical Olley–Pakes framework assumptions to multidimensional productivity and then develop an identification strategy based on a control variable approach and first‐order conditions. I use this method to estimate output elasticities and markups in manufacturing industries in the US and four developing countries. I find that neglecting labor‐augmenting productivity underestimates capital elasticity, overestimates variable input elasticity, and overestimates markups in all countries.

title: Informal Redistribution Through Work
authors: Elisa Macchi, Jeremia Stalder
abstract: We investigate work as informal redistribution, leveraging field experiments and firm‐level survey data from Kampala, Uganda. Employers and workers consistently choose redistribution through work over cash transfers, revealing a willingness to pay for work. By randomizing work tasks—some designed to have zero marginal product—we find that production value does not explain these choices: employers pay for zero‐value work. These patterns are also inconsistent with other relational benefits, such as social image concerns or networking. Instead, motivations are normative. Experimental evidence reveals an internalized norm for redistribution through work rooted in incentive arguments on the demand side—as employers stop requiring work only when workers have verifiable emergencies—and in reciprocity and dignity from earning on the supply side. The norm shapes both the organization and measurement of production: failing to account for redistribution through work makes firms appear significantly larger and less productive than they are.

title: Two‐Sided Markets Shaped by Platform‐Guided Search
authors: Kwok Hao Lee, Leon Musolff
abstract: This paper investigates concerns that vertically integrated platforms like Amazon steer demand toward their own offers via algorithmic prominence, potentially harming consumers. On Amazon, for each product, the Buybox prominence algorithm selects one seller to feature, influencing which offers consumers consider. Using novel Amazon sales and Buybox (prominence) data, we estimate a structural model capturing the effects of such algorithmic prominence on consumer choices, seller pricing, and entry. We find that the platform can indeed steer demand as 95% of consumers consider only the Buybox offer. The Buybox is highly price‐elastic (−21), but skews toward Amazon's own offers, which are featured as frequently as observably similar offers priced 5% cheaper. Still, as consumers prefer these offers, this skew does not amount to self‐preferencing in the sense of harming consumers: consumer surplus is roughly maximized at the estimated Amazon Buybox advantage, which balances higher prices against showing consumers their preferred offers.

title: Extreme Value Theory With Heterogeneous Agents
authors: Sephorah Mangin
abstract: Extreme value processes feature in any economic model in which agents receive a number of draws from some distribution of values and we examine the behavior of the maximum value in the limit as the number of draws becomes large. This paper asks: Do the average outcomes of such processes change when different agents receive a different number of draws? To answer this, we allow the number of draws an agent receives from the underlying distribution of values (e.g., productivities, ideas, or utility shocks) to be given by a search technology , which reflects heterogeneity in the expected number of draws across different types of agents. We derive a new class of extreme value distributions that generalizes the three standard distributions (Fréchet, Gumbel, Weibull) by incorporating heterogeneity across agents. We generalize a result from Gabaix, Laibson, Li, Li, Resnick, and de Vries (2016) regarding extreme value outcomes and consider applications to aggregate productivity, markups, and social networks.

title: The Social Learning Barrier
authors: Florian Brandl
abstract: Long‐lived agents interact repeatedly in a social network. In each period, each agent observes a private signal, chooses an action, and then observes the actions of her neighbors. We show that the learning rate of the slowest‐learning agent is capped by a constant that depends only on the distribution of the most informative private signal, but not on the number of agents, the network structure, correlations between the private signals, or the agents' strategies. For equilibrium learning with rational agents, the same result bounds the learning rate of every agent in any equilibrium under a broad class of conditions. The result is driven by an information‐theoretic tradeoff between optimal action choices and information revelation.

title: An Exact t ‐Test
authors: Guillaume A. Pouliot
abstract: Multivariate linear regression and randomization‐based inference are two essential methods in statistics and econometrics. Nevertheless, the problem of producing a randomized test for the value of a single regression coefficient that is exactly valid when errors are exchangeable, and which is asymptotically valid for the best linear predictor, has remained elusive. In this paper, we produce a test that is exactly valid with exchangeable errors and which allows for general covariate designs; covariates may be continuous as well as discrete and may be correlated. The test is asymptotically valid when the errors are not exchangeable, in particular in the presence of conditional heteroskedasticity.

title: From Predictive Algorithms to the Automatic Generation of Anomalies
authors: Sendhil Mullainathan, Ashesh Rambachan
abstract: How can we extract theoretical insights from machine learning algorithms? We take a familiar lesson: researchers often turn intuition into theoretical insight by constructing “anomalies”—specific examples highlighting hypothesized flaws in a theory, such as the Allais paradox. We develop procedures that replace researchers' intuitions with predictive algorithms: given a predictive algorithm and a theory, our procedures automatically generate anomalies for that theory. We illustrate our procedures by generating anomalies for expected utility theory. Based on a neural network that accurately predicts lottery choices, we recover known anomalies for expected utility theory and discover novel ones. In incentivized experiments, subjects violate expected utility theory on these algorithmically generated anomalies at rates similar to the Allais paradox and common ratio effect.

title: Coalitions in Repeated Games
authors: S. Nageeb Ali, Ce Liu
abstract: This paper proposes a framework and solution concept for repeated coalitional behavior. We model history‐dependent schemes that use continuation promises and punishments to deter coalitions from blocking. We evaluate the effectiveness of these schemes with and without transferable utility, and apply the framework to study the implications of wage transparency in labor markets.

title: Intermediate Input Substitutability
authors: Alessandra Peter, Cian Ruane
abstract: We estimate long‐run elasticities of substitution between intermediate inputs for Indian manufacturing plants. India's trade liberalization in the early 1990s provides an ideal natural policy experiment, with permanent and heterogeneous tariff reductions inducing changes in relative prices which we use for identification. We find a high degree of substitutability at the plant‐level between 8 broad categories of material inputs, significantly above the Cobb–Douglas benchmark of 1. In contrast, when considering shorter time horizons or more transitory shocks to relative prices, we find evidence of much lower elasticities. Using our long‐run elasticities in a quantitative model, we find that misallocation of intermediate inputs causes a reduction in aggregate output of 29%–3.5 times larger relative to a standard calibration with complementary inputs.

title: DP22208 Inference from Outcomes in the Market for Lemons
authors: Francesc Dilme, Nenad Kos
abstract: This paper studies inference from equilibrium outcomes in a market for lemons. A monopsonist posts a price to sellers who privately observe the quality of their goods. An analyst knows preferences and observes the price and quantity traded. Combining the observed quantity with the optimality of the price, we characterize rationalizable outcomes and derive sharp bounds on the quality distribution, producer surplus, con- sumer surplus, total welfare, and deadweight loss. Comparing two buyer valuation functions, we show that a pointwise higher valuation shrinks the set of rationalizable outcomes but expands the range of producer surplus at any outcome rationalizable under both. When the buyer’s utility is independent of quality, the model reduces to standard monopoly pricing, and first-order stochastic-dominance bounds characterize rationalizing distributions. These characterizations extend to observations of the price alone.

title: DP22207 The Third Great Transition: From Human-Bound to Autonomous AI-Driven Innovation
authors: Oded Galor
abstract: Why haven't advances in AI accelerated aggregate productivity growth? Could an apparently stable balanced-growth regime conceal an impending phase transition that would trigger the Third Great Transition in human history, following the Neolithic and Industrial Revolutions? This research advances the hypothesis that the AI Revolution will unleash a phase transition in which the prevailing balanced-growth regime and its gravitational pull will vanish, while a radically faster growth trajectory will emerge as a new attractor, bringing about a profound metamorphosis of the growth process. It advances a dynamic theory of the AI Revolution in which a deceptively stable balanced-growth regime endogenously generates the conditions for its own demise. As diminishing returns to AI advances relative to the technological frontier align the growth rates of technological knowledge and AI capability, aggregate productivity growth may remain stable. Yet absolute AI capability advances relentlessly toward the cognitive threshold that unleashes autonomous AI-driven innovation, fundamentally transforming the engine of innovation. Recursive AI improvement propels the economy toward either a substantially higher balanced-growth path or a regime of perpetually accelerating growth. Beneath the deceptive calm of stable productivity growth lies the inexorable buildup of transformative forces, destined to unleash an unprecedented transformation of the human condition.

title: DP22206 The Mechanisms of Historical Persistence
authors: Morgan Kelly
abstract: What do persistence coefficients actually measure? When the underlying behavioural mechanism causes observations to evolve as a vector autoregression (VAR) it is shown that persistence coefficients do not measure “the legacy of the past.” While the maximum duration of deviations from equilibrium is given by the spectral radius of the VAR, the persistence regression also captures permanent differences in steady states between locations, with the result that their coefficients can seriously overestimate the persistence of the underlying behavioural process. (This problem extends to any cross-sectional or panel regression with a lagged dependent variable, including tests of Solow convergence, price rigidity or the inter-generational transmission of wealth or IQ.) Turning to estimation, in the presence of small common shocks t-statistics are shown to diverge, consistent with the spurious significance that appears endemic in the field. Finally, a disquieting number of the foundational results in historical persistence rest on the omission of obvious controls or lapses in basic econometrics.

title: DP22209 Beyond the First-Best: Welfare and OPEC Market Power
authors: Jan De Loecker, John Asker, Allan Collard-Wexler, Charlotte De Cannière
abstract: We introduce an empirical framework to quantify the welfare impact of market power, through coordinated production decisions by a cartel, while allowing for other distortions. We contrast two novel concepts – the marginal and the infra-marginal welfare loss – to a naive approach that fails to recognize the existence of other distortions operating alongside market power. We apply the framework to measure the impact of market power of OPEC in the global crude oil market. We leverage unique micro data on cost and production to quantify the deadweight loss and productive inefficiency due to the OPEC cartel. From 1970 onward, the naive approach implies that OPEC generated 2.2 trillion dollars of welfare losses, two-thirds from productive inefficiency and one-third from deadweight loss. Eliminating cost-minimization violations outside the cartel shrinks losses to around 0.7 trillion dollars, indicating that other frictions in the oil market are complementary to OPEC’s market power.

title: DP22202 Intermediaries, Quality Incentives, and Upgrading along Supply Chains
authors: Jie Bai, Lauren Falcao Bergquist, Ameet Morjaria, Russell Morton, Yulu Tang
programme: Development Economics, Industrial Organization, Organizational Economics
abstract: Many low-income countries remain concentrated in low-quality production despite substantial quality premiums in world markets. We study how domestic intermediaries connecting producers to these markets shape incentives for quality upgrading and where it occurs along supply chains. In Uganda’s coffee industry, we collect transaction-level prices and lab-based quality measures along the chain. We document that the quality premium falls by roughly half from the export gate to the farm gate. We develop a model in which intermediaries' buyer power and their own upgrading can both compress the premium. Buyer power distorts upgrading incentives and shifts profits away from farmers, while intermediary upgrading adds value and can benefit farmers by raising demand for low-quality coffee. To disentangle these mechanisms, we run a field experiment offering randomized, quality-contingent production contracts to farmers and intermediaries to separately identify costs and markdowns. We find that buyer power plays the larger role in compressing the quality premium and reducing farmer welfare, while intermediary upgrading benefits farmers and matters most for aggregate high-quality output. Because these effects pull in opposite directions, counterfactuals show that “cutting out the middleman,” often proposed to curb intermediary market power, involves a trade-off: it raises farmer profits but sharply reduces high-quality exports. By contrast, easing intermediaries’ entry into high-quality trade strengthens competition and expands their upgrading, raising both farmer profits and high-quality exports.

title: DP22204 Economic Literacy: Measurement, Expectations, and Policy Views
authors: Raphael Brade, Henning Hermes, Tim Kaiser, Sarah Necker, Anke Windisch, Ludger Woessmann
abstract: How important is economic literacy – the understanding of basic economic concepts – for the formation of economic expectations and policy views? We design, implement, and psychometrically validate a survey module to measure economic literacy in a representative adult population. Economic literacy is associated with education and intelligence but captures a distinct skill. While unrelated to ideological orientation, individuals with higher economic literacy (1) hold better-anchored economic expectations, (2) are more responsive to experimentally provided information on policy trade-offs, and (3) show a closer alignment between preferences, policy views, and party support. The results are consistent with economic literacy enabling voters to better process information and form policy views more consistent with their underlying preferences.

title: DP22205 The Limits of Behavioral Simulation with AI
authors: Thomas Graeber, Christopher Roth
abstract: How well can we simulate human behavior with AI? We review over 100 studies to ask what the evidence means for credible use cases. First, how accurate are simulations where they have been checked against human data? Accuracy falls with specificity: simulations often get the direction and ranking of well-documented effects right but are far less reliable about effect sizes when simulating respondents, and about response distributions, subgroup differences, and individual choices. Second, does accuracy measured in one setting transfer to new settings, where simulation is most useful but cannot be checked? Accuracy sometimes transfers within familiar task families, but evidence beyond them is scarce and mostly negative. The evidence is consistent with simulations drawing on a reduced-form account of what has been written about people rather than a structural model of behavior. Better models do not resolve the transfer question, because their accuracy can only be measured where human data exist. We discuss the promise of three possible approaches to improve performance in new settings. Adding behavioral theory carries predictions beyond the training data, but only as far as the theory is accurate and complete. Additional training on behavior from settings just like the one of interest improves simulation only if they are highly similar in kind. Human data close to the context of interest can instead be used to directly measure and correct simulation error in the target setting, which transfers only as long as the error structure stays similar.

title: DP22203 Postal Votes
authors: Torun Dewan, Kfir Eliaz
abstract: Postal voting lowers participation costs but can make votes purchasable. We study competing parties offering enforceable payments to voters whose preferences and voting costs are private. Uncertainty about allegiance and preference intensity limits vote buying, since offers may reward supporters or fail to persuade opponents. We derive sufficient conditions under which postal voting increases sincere turnout, the share of citizens voting for their preferred party, despite active purchases and preference reversals. More precise allegiance signals need not increase reversals. Under a sufficient condition, we construct an equilibrium family along which sincere turnout decreases with precision once vote buying becomes active.

title: DP22196 Trade Policy for National Security: Dependence, Scarcity Rents, and Capacity
authors: Aurélien Eyquem, Gianluca Benigno
abstract: When a foreign economy is more efficient at producing an essential good, the domestic economy can import it cheaply but may lose access in a disruption. How much domestic productive capacity should firms install? We characterize a national-security capacity externality: anticipated emergency redistribution can prevent domestic producers from appropriating the scarcity premium when imports fail. Essentiality and disruption risk alone create no capacity distortion: with full appropriation, free trade is constrained efficient. In a small open economy, an implementing tariff can close the capacity wedge, while a capacity payment also avoids the tariff’s consumption distortion. In two-country general equilibrium, we separate this national-security motive from conventional terms-of-trade incentives. With both instruments available, the payment corrects the capacity wedge and the tariff addresses market power. When foreign policymakers can choose disruption risk, the prospect of a terms-of-trade gain can make positive risk attractive. In our illustrative calibration, we find equilibria with positive risk and protection when appropriation is sufficiently limited, yet both countries lose relative to no-risk free trade. These outcomes depend on appropriation, comparative advantage and relative country size.

title: DP22201 The China Shock and Employment Concentration within Local Labor Markets
authors: Rosario Crinò
programme: International Trade and Regional Economics, Macroeconomics and Growth
abstract: This paper studies whether Chinese import penetration changed the internal geography of U.S. local labor markets. Using granular workplace employment data for 2002-2020 and the instrumental-variable design of Autor et al. (2013), I find that Chinese import penetration reduced employment concentration within commuting zones. An interquartile increase in import exposure explains about 15% of the differential decline in the Herfindahl-Hirschman index. Looking across employment nodes within commuting zones, I find that this decline reflects a disproportionate reduction in the employment shares of initially dominant nodes. This pattern is closely linked to sectoral composition: nodes with greater initial manufacturing presence experienced larger relative declines in employment shares, and differences in manufacturing presence account for a substantial part of the size gradient in these within-CZ responses. The results document a spatial margin of adjustment to trade shocks that is not captured by aggregate local employment outcomes.

title: DP22199 Last-Mile Delivery and the Future of Foreign Aid
authors: Erika Deserranno, Andrea Guariso, Nancy Qian
abstract: Foreign aid seeks to provide basic services, such as health care and education, to poor and vulnerable populations. Its effectiveness depends on last-mile delivery: whether those services reach the people who need them. This article reviews evidence on two key aspects of last-mile delivery. The first concerns the growing role of non-state providers, especially NGOs, and its implications for the state’s capacity to deliver services and coordinate across providers. The second concerns the selection, motivation, and management of frontline workers who provide the services directly to beneficiaries. We argue that decisions about aid allocation and withdrawal should account for the need to preserve last-mile delivery capacity, which takes time and resources to build but can quickly erode.

title: DP22198 Testing Times: Reputation for Debt Discipline
authors: Anton Tsoy
abstract: How do countries build a reputation for debt discipline? I develop a continuous-time model in which an impatient government, whose income follows a jump-diffusion process, finances consumption by issuing long-term debt to patient investors. The opportunistic government cannot commit to future debt policies and builds reputation by mimicking a commitment type that maintains a stable debt-to-income ratio. I characterize a Markov perfect equilibrium in closed form. Reputation building is slow and confined to "testing times," episodes of large negative shocks when debt reduction becomes a credible signal of commitment. Reputation building is path-dependent and risky: a single large shock builds reputation faster than a sequence of smaller ones but it also can destroy reputation. Because reputation is built through disciplined debt management rather than timely repayment, its loss need not trigger immediate default. Instead, it shifts bondholders' expectations about future debt policy, generating divergent paths for countries that maintain reputation and those that lose it. With positive reputation, debt prices decouple from fundamentals and are determined by accumulated reputation. Without reputation, bondholders anticipate continuous issuance and dilution, so debt prices become sensitive to current debt ratios.

title: DP22200 Gender Disparities in the Welfare Effect of the Minimum Wage
authors: Decio Coviello, Erika Deserranno, Nicola Persico
abstract: We study how women and men working in the same minimum-wage supported job respond to, and benefit from, a minimum wage increase. Using administrative data from a major US retailer, we find that the welfare of women increases less with the minimum wage hike than that of men, even though both attain comparable pay raises. We show that this occurs because women exert more effort in response to the minimum wage increase, driven by their greater need for job retention due to less favorable outside options. This evidence points to a generalizable mechanism whereby disparities outside the firm account for welfare disparities in the impact of an important gender-neutral policy (i.e., the minimum wage) inside the firm.

title: DP22197 Valuing the Cost of Incomplete Global Markets
authors: Karen K. Lewis, Edith Liu
programme: International Macroeconomics and Finance, Asset Pricing
abstract: Deviations from complete financial markets in cross-border investments generate economic welfare costs. This paper shows how to value these costs using standard theory and data based on three main results. Our first result shows how welfare valuations can be derived from a general wealth-to-dividend ratio. Next, we establish how aggregate consumption and exchange rate data can be used to uncover diversifiable goods allocations across countries. Finally, we demonstrate how asset pricing data and models can be used to value deviations from complete markets. The paper outlines a range of applications that fall under this framework, including financial intermediary constraint models.

title: DP22195 Cost Evidence and Welfare in Optimal Procurement
authors: Patrick W. Schmitz
abstract: A buyer seeks to procure a good or service from one of two ex ante identical suppliers who privately know their costs and whether they possess evidence verifying those costs. We characterize profit-maximizing procurement mechanisms with and without admissible cost evidence. Allowing evidence weakly raises buyer profit but can reduce total surplus, even when procurement becomes more frequent. The optimal mechanism favors evidence holders and may select a more costly supplier. Allowing cost evidence improves welfare for sufficiently small procurement benefits and lowers it for sufficiently large benefits.

title: DP22194 The Firm as a Cultivator of Internal Relationships: How Rotation Supports Favor Exchanges in Organizations
authors: Nicholas Argyres, Giorgio Zanarone
abstract: In a multidivisional firm, units must frequently transfer resources to each other to address unforeseen contingencies. Yet, the organization typically lacks the information to enforce unscheduled resource transfers, and divisions lack the budgetary discretion to pay for them. We model interdivisional cooperation as a “favor-exchange” agreement in which a division’s manager may transfer resources to another division in the hope of being a receiver in the future. We show that by reassigning managers to roles over time, the organization can facilitate internal favor-exchange agreements. We derive conditions under which role rotation makes the promise of interdivisional favor exchanges more credible by increasing the managers’ future rewards from cooperation (rotation across divisions) or the punishment they suffer after defection (rotation in and out of superior positions). We discuss empirical implications of the model, as well as applications to other kinds of organizations such as government agencies, buyer-supplier relationships, and strategic alliances.

title: DP22193 Does the Stock Market Price Operational Flexibility?
authors: Li Li, Xiangyang Li, Steven Ongena, Yabin Wang
abstract: We examine whether stock markets value firms’ operational flexibility by exploiting the unexpected 2015 Tianjin Port explosion. Using pre-event shipment records, we identify exposed U.S. listed firms independently of corporate disruption announcements. Firms with broader geographic operations and supply-chain networks experience smaller losses, while China-related executive connections are associated with more modest immediate declines after the explosion. Our findings suggest that investors value operating alternatives and local knowledge already in place. The value of operational flexibility extends beyond firms’ own facilities to their external networks and relationships.

title: DP22192 Stock Lending and Pass-Through Voting
authors: Doron Levit, George Nurisso
abstract: Concerns about conflicts of interest have led to growing calls for asset managers to let fund investors cast votes directly at shareholder meetings. We study this reform, known as pass-through voting, in a model where market participants with heterogeneous preferences lend shares, trade, and vote. We show that it can move voting outcomes further away from investors’ preferences, rather than closer, for a reason that has received little attention: the fund's manager retains control over share lending and may lend more once the votes are no longer his to cast. Because the votes attached to lent shares end up in the hands of traders whose preferences differ from those of the fund’s investors, pass-through voting can leave these investors worse off, even after accounting for lending revenue. The manager, meanwhile, may embrace the reform to increase lending income. Our analyses inform the debate over mandating pass-through voting, the use of lending fees as a proxy for the value of a vote, and, more broadly, policy at the intersection of shareholder voting and securities lending.

title: DP22191 Permanence and Performance: Temporary Contracts and Worker Effort
authors: Zihan Hu, Hyejin Ku, Xuan Wang, Xinjue Yao
abstract: Can the prospect of permanent employment motivate worker effort under temporary contracts? We use daily production records from a Chinese garment factory where conversion to permanent contracts leaves piece rates and core tasks unchanged. Among workers who successfully convert, daily output falls by about 5 percent on average in the nine months after the conversion announcement. The decline is larger for workers with weaker outside options. A sister plant in Vietnam, where conversion was universal after two years of service, shows no comparable decline. These findings suggest that uncertainty about obtaining permanent employment induces additional effort under temporary contracts.

title: DP22190 Monopsonistic Search
authors: Pietro Garibaldi, Espen Rasmus Moen, Enrico Duilio Turri
abstract: We develop a search-and-matching model in which firms can influence the flow of recruits by posting higher wages. Workers draw a privately observed match-specific amenity cost on contact, so the firm's recruiting probability is increasing in its own wage, giving rise to monopsony power. We show that the decentralized equilibrium is inefficient: a marginal wage increase raises aggregate welfare, and may increase employment. If amenities are drawn from a constant-elasticity distribution, the model can be calibrated using aggregate data only. Calibrated to United States data for 2022--2024, the model implies an inverse acceptance elasticity of 2.9, a wage markdown of 14 percent, and a welfare-maximizing wage 10 percent above the decentralized level. We extend the model to account for fiscal externalities and show that the efficient wage is still 9.5 percent higher than the monopsonistic wage.

title: DP22186 Antitrust, Market Power, and U.S. Economic Outcomes
authors: Brian Amorim Cabaco, Morten Ravn
abstract: We assemble a narrative record of all federal antitrust case filings by the DoJ and FTC since the mid-1950s. We document a shift from civil non-merger and criminal enforcement toward civil merger cases in the early 1980s. Non-merger and criminal filings reduce defendants' markups while increasing sales and input expenditure. We construct sector-level enforcement proxies from publicly listed defendants' stock-market reactions to filings. Increased enforcement strengthens competition, raises output, R&D capital and patenting, and improves allocative efficiency. For civil non-merger and criminal cases, output gains are accompanied by greater input use. For civil merger cases, output rises without sustained increases in inputs, consistent with a role for productivity and resource allocation.

title: DP22184 Behavioral Bias, Relative to What? Robustness and Discounting in a Bewley Economy
authors: Lars Peter Hansen, Francesco Lippi, Thomas Sargent
abstract: We construct a linear-quadratic Bewley economy whose consumers differ in discount factors (patience) and concerns about misspecification (robustness). We solve in closed form for a locus on which less patience offsets more robustness, so every type’s consumption-saving rule coincides with that of a benchmark consumer who trusts his model. Any distribution of types on the locus supports the same interest rate and joint distribution of consumption, debt, and income. Quantity data do not separately identify patience and robustness, even when the endowment law is known. Types difer in worst-case forecasts, shadow prices, and welfare evaluations, but all satisfy an Euler-equation restriction testable with elicited data. We bound admissible heterogeneity and compute detection error probabilities. Measured from the benchmark, a robust consumer looks pessimistic and impatient; from another type, he can look optimistic and patient. Attributing a behavioral bias therefore requires a reference model that quantity data do not select.

title: DP22189 Frontier Technology in Frontier Markets? Financing Global AI Entrepreneurship
authors: GIlles Q. Hacheme, Ebehi Iyoha, Abdoulaye Ndiaye, Noureini S. Souleymane
programme: Development Economics, Macroeconomics and Growth, Banking and Corporate Finance
abstract: Does the global diffusion of artificial intelligence (AI) extend to the creation and financing of the firms that build it? Using a novel dataset of 116,795 startups founded between 2015 and 2022 across 172 countries, we link company descriptions and financing histories to the employment and education records of founders, early employees, and potential investors. We document a stark divergence between the real and financial sides of global AI entrepreneurship. On the real side, AI startups everywhere display the hallmarks of a general-purpose technology: in every world region, they target more customer sectors than comparable non-AI startups and are more likely to sell horizontal products that apply across industries. Moreover, following the release of ChatGPT, startups whose baseline tasks were more amenable to AI expanded the breadth of their work activities and commercial staffing. Yet the financing advantage that such scalable businesses command is sharply localized. AI startups raise 151 percent more annual capital than non-AI peers in North America and 181 percent more in the Middle East, compared with 42 percent more in East Asia, 16 percent more in Europe, and no detectable premium in Africa, Latin America, or South Asia. Accounting for targeted customer markets, founder credentials, early-team human capital, and local investor characteristics explains part of the gap in Latin America but leaves the broader global divide intact. In Africa, half of all AI funding goes to basic compute and data-center infrastructure; excluding these providers reveals that African AI product startups raise 57 percent less than non-AI peers. These patterns provide an early warning that AI may reach users around the world without building firms around the world.

title: DP22187 The Changing Vulnerability of the U.S. Economy to Oil Shocks
authors: Danilo Leiva-Leon, Giovanni Olivei, Ara Patvakanian, Jenny Tang, Egon Zakrajšek
abstract: The United States has gone from heavy oil dependence to being a net petroleum exporter. Time-varying parameter regressions show the macroeconomic association with oil price increases has weakened, especially for employment. State-level instrumental variables local projections suggest a source: an oil supply shock raising the real oil price by 1 standard deviation lifts employment in a state at the 90th percentile of oil production intensity by about 0.2 percentage point more over two years than in a non-producing state. These relative gains, visible in non-extraction employment and house prices, point to regional offsets that may dampen the aggregate inflation–real activity tradeoff.

title: DP22185 Creative Destruction with AI versus AI's Destruction of Creativity
authors: Christian Bayer, Petr Sedláček
abstract: Debates about AI have largely focused on its effects on productivity within existing firms or tasks. We argue that a key question for long-run welfare is whether AI will itself generate new ideas and products. Using a model of firm entry and selection where product development is uncertain and exclusively human-led, we show that AI automation may reduce welfare, even if it also raises productivity. This happens because automation erodes private returns that help justify investment into new ideas. Therefore, higher AI-induced productivity need not increase welfare if it undermines Schumpeterian incentives for creativity.

title: DP22188 Remote Work and Monetary Policy
authors: Petr Sedláček, Chenchuan Shi
abstract: After the pandemic, remote work surged alongside tight labor markets. We study the monetary policy implications of this pattern in a New Keynesian model with hiring frictions and optimal remote work choices. Better remote work conditions raise employment surplus and hiring, lowering the natural unemployment rate. Central banks which learn about this change gradually, misperceive the labor market as tight and run the economy cold. Estimating learning speed using FOMC projection revisions, we find that misperception costs are as large as 15 years of business cycle fluctuations. Our results support less weight on unemployment when its natural rate is uncertain.

title: DP22183 Partisan Demographics
authors: Damilola Afolabi, Klaus F. Zimmermann
abstract: This chapter defines and reviews partisan demographics as an emerging field at the intersection of political demography, political economy, and population economics. Whereas political demography examines how population change affects politics, partisan demographics studies how political events, party control, political climates, and policy regimes influence demographic behavior in ways that vary with the partisan alignment of individuals, households, or local populations. The chapter asks under what conditions partisan events become demographic shocks and organizes the evidence around five mechanisms: economic expectations, policy anticipation, affective identity, social matching and sorting, and risk perception and health behavior. The strongest evidence currently concerns fertility and reproductive behavior, including conceptions and abortions, while studies of marriage, partnership formation, residential sorting, health behavior, wellbeing, and mortality extend the field with varying degrees of empirical support. Evidence on migration, integration, and naturalization remains more limited. Particular attention is given to empirical credibility, including the timing of political shocks and demographic responses, the distinction between behavior and attitudes, the measurement of partisan exposure, and the separation of partisan effects from pre-existing demographic differences. The chapter concludes by identifying the conditions under which partisan politics becomes a consequential determinant of demographic behavior and by outlining priorities for future research.

title: DP22181 Does Peter Piper Pick Pepper Inattentively? Consumer Inattention to Package Content
authors: Laura Grigolon, Ian Meeker, Jakob von Ditfurth
abstract: We study consumer inattention to product downsizing, whereby manufacturers raise unit prices by reducing package content. We develop a novel method to recover inattention within a random coefficient discrete choice framework. Applying our method to the pepper industry, where thirty downsizing episodes affected a third of category sales, we find that almost no consumers notice downsizing and that they are more sensitive to package prices than to net weight. Making downsizing salient raises consumer surplus, while banning downsizing generates only half as much consumer surplus gain because restoring package content raises marginal costs and hence prices.

title: DP22182 How does AI distribute the Pie?
authors: Douglas Araujo, Harald Uhlig
abstract: As Large Language Models (LLMs) increasingly advise financial decisions and undertake autonomous decision-making, understanding their strategic choices is crucial. We study LLM choices in the Ultimatum Game, a setting where humans deviate from theoretical rationality. We vary stakes and opponent types (Human vs. AI) across Proposer and Responder roles. Three results emerge. First, LLM behavior is heterogeneous but predictable conditional on the stakes and agent type. Second, while rational profit-maximization and human-like choices occur, a distinct “altruistic” mode with high distribution shares emerges. Third, LLM reasoning is puzzling to a human observer: these altruistic offers actually reflect acceptance risk.

title: DP22179 Divide and Indebt How Geoeconomic Fragmentation Affects Public Debt and Macro-Fiscal Stability
authors: Davide Furceri, Marcos Poplawski-Ribeiro, Ervin Prifti
abstract: This paper quantifies the macro-fiscal consequences of geoeconomic fragmentation using the Geopolitical Fragmentation Index of Fernández Villaverde, Mineyama, and Song (2024). Using a panel of 90 economies over 1990-2022, we identify structural fragmentation shocks in a panel SVAR and trace their dynamic effects through local projections, allowing for heterogeneity across country groups. We find that a one standard deviation increase in geoeconomic fragmentation raises public debt by up to 3 percentage points of GDP in the medium term. The debt buildup reflects weaker economic activity, wider fiscal deficits driven by higher spending and lower revenues, and a temporary tightening of financing conditions. The effects are stronger in advanced economies and in countries more exposed to geopolitically distant trade partners. Geoeconomic fragmentation also amplifies uncertainty around future debt and growth and increases the risk of tail events.

title: DP22173 A Closely-Held View of Dividend Taxation
authors: Laurent Bach, Antoine Bozio, Arthur Guillouzouic, Claire Leroy, Clément Malgouyres
abstract: This paper introduces a ``closely-held view'' of dividend taxation, departing from traditional views fitting widely-held firms. Firms' owner-managers choose between distributing and retaining profits, and rarely issue equity, such that dividend taxes affect payouts but not investment. We test this view using two French reforms that raised dividend taxes in 2013 and cut them in 2018. Exploiting matched shareholder-firm tax data, we find very large dividend tax elasticities, with most of the response coming from closely-held firms. In line with this view, investment is insensitive to dividend taxation. Instead, changes in payouts are absorbed by retained earnings, reflecting that owner-managers treat their firms as low-tax saving vehicles.

title: DP22174 Thin Markets, Thick Subsidies: Local Competition and the Incidence of Heat Pump Grants
authors: Shefali Khanna, Ralf Martin, Florian Münch, Aurélien Saussay
programme: Public Economics, Climate Change and the Environment
abstract: We study how local supply shapes the incidence and quantity response of clean-technology subsidies. In October 2023, the UK government increased the grant for air-source heat pumps from £5,000 to £7,500 in England and Wales, while Scotland left its policy unchanged. Using 260,000 certified heat pump installation records in a difference-in-differences comparison of Northern England with Scotland, we find that the grant increase raised monthly installations by 24%, adding roughly 7,200 units over 20 post-reform months. Reported pre-grant installation costs fell by about £830, so household out-of-pocket payments declined by more than the £2,500 grant increase. The quantity expansion and the cost reduction were larger in local areas with more competition prior to the policy. Supply adjusted through local installer entry, wider geographic reach among existing installers, and a shift toward smaller, higher-efficiency heat pumps. While changes in heat pump size and model mix explain roughly half of the unconditional cost drop, within-installer-and-model price cuts account for a quarter of the average decline and half of the additional price drop in more competitive markets. Combining these estimates with engineering-based carbon abatement yields a marginal value of public funds of 2.1, rising to 2.5 in markets one standard deviation above mean competition.

title: DP22172 School Choice and Educational Inputs: Unintended Consequences of a Targeted Voucher Program
authors: Olivier De Groote, Ana Gazmuri
programme: Industrial Organization, Labour Economics, Public Economics
abstract: We estimate a novel education production function on a large observational dataset in a context with school choice. Using data from Chile, we estimate heterogeneous effects of class size, teacher experience and financial inputs, while allowing for unobserved school, student, and teacher characteristics to be correlated with them. We then use this model to decompose the channels behind the increase in test scores in both private and public schools, following a voucher reform. The reform increased financial inputs but also caused many students to leave public schools, leading to a passive decrease in class size and a drop in teacher experience. We find large heterogeneity in effects and show that the increase in financial inputs explains an important part of the test score increases through their positive effects in the best public schools. The drop in class size helped worse-performing public schools, while the large drop in teacher experience had negligible effects for all schools. Effects in private schools were more homogeneous and inputs more stable.

title: DP22180 Weathering the Energy Crisis: Can Tailored Information to Local Governments and Media Spur Climate Action?
authors: Menna Bishop, Immanuel Feld, Thiemo Fetzer, Ludovica Gazzè
abstract: Can evidence tailored to local public actors, that is policy makers and media, increase residential energy efficiency investments? During the 2022 energy crisis, we randomly assigned local authorities in England and Wales to an outreach treatment. Councillors, council officers, and local media in treated authorities received localized estimates of household exposure to rising energy prices and potential savings from retrofits. Treatment increased retrofit installations by 7 percent, mainly through solar photovoltaics, with no detectable change in energy consumption. Installations were concentrated near councilors' homes, a pattern consistent with local diffusion of the information through policy makers.

title: DP22177 The Global Fiscal Actions (GFA) Dataset
authors: Hites Ahir, Matthieu Bellon, Maria Chiara Cavalleri, Shuvam Das, Davide Furceri, Faizaan Kisat, Aiko Mineshima, Irene Rausell Moreno, Vishal Parmar, Nikhil Patel, Adrian Peralta-Alva
abstract: We introduce the Global Fiscal Actions (GFA) Dataset, the first quarterly global narrative database of discretionary fiscal policy actions, covering 142 countries since 1990. GFA combines Economist Intelligence Unit country reports with large language models to systematically identify and classify tax and spending measures, together with their motivations, timing, implementation status, and supporting evidence. We validate the dataset against economists' assessments, existing narrative datasets, fiscal aggregates, and repeated AI extractions, demonstrating high accuracy and reproducibility. We illustrate its value through applications to fiscal cyclicality and country-specific fiscal multipliers, providing new evidence on the conduct and effectiveness of fiscal policy worldwide.

title: DP22176 Redistribution, Institutions, and the Self-Selection of Migrants
authors: Leoluca Villa, Giacomo Corneo, Guido Neidhofer
abstract: In the face of slow productivity growth, labor shortages and concerns about brain drain, welfare states seek to understand how policies influence the skill composition of migrants. Using administrative data on the universe of Italians residing abroad, this paper investigates how governmental redistribution and institutional quality shape migration decisions across 45 main destination countries. We find that higher levels of income redistribution are associated with more negative skill selection. Access to human-capital–enhancing public services and higher institutional quality are instead linked to a more positive selection. The latter effects are economically significant and potentially able to offset the adverse effects from redistribution. Complementary quasi-experimental evidence exploiting a drastic deterioration of institutional quality in Italy during the Berlusconi years corroborates these findings. Overall, the evidence suggests that, to the extent that they improve how effectively and equitably they use public resources, welfare states are able to attract a balanced selection of migrants despite high levels of income redistribution.

title: DP22175 The Message or the Messenger? Scientific Evidence and Policy Misperceptions
authors: Marco Bertoni, Paolo Falco, Luigi Guiso, Tullio Jappelli, Roberto Nisticò
abstract: Citizens learn about the effects of public policies mainly through news media, and their beliefs often diverge from the available scientific evidence. Using a survey experiment on a representative sample of around 5,000 Italian residents, we study whether exposure to scientific evidence corrects misperceptions about four salient and politically contested reforms, and whether belief updating depends on the political alignment between individuals and the media outlet conveying the evidence. To separate the message from the messenger, respondents see the same piece of real, non-deceptive scientific evidence, while we randomize whether it is reported by unspecified outlets, a left-leaning newspaper, or a right-leaning newspaper. Misperceptions are widespread, and providing scientific evidence shifts beliefs toward accuracy. Crucially, updating is largely independent of source alignment: across all four reforms, credible evidence can travel across partisan divides, so the partisan branding of a mainstream outlet is not the primary barrier to communicating evaluated policy effects.

title: DP22178 Global Shocks and Insulation: Evidence from the Middle East and North Africa
authors: Michele Castegini, Giancarlo Corsetti, Zeina Hasna, Simon Lloyd, Nadine Yamout
programme: International Macroeconomics and Finance, Monetary Economics and Fluctuations
abstract: We study the transmission of U.S. monetary policy shocks to 18 Middle East, North Africa, and Pakistan (MENAP) economies over 1990–2025, using state-dependent local projections, and find two main results. First, on its own, exchange-rate flexibility offers only limited insulation to external shocks in the short-to-medium run. Following a U.S. monetary policy shock, activity is significantly better protected in crawling regimes than under fixed pegs; but not fully flexible regimes, where activity contracts significantly. Insulation therefore appears non-monotonic in the degree of exchange-rate volatility, rather than increasing with it as the classic Mundell-Fleming view suggests. Second, however, we find no evidence of a breakdown in the exchange rate’s role in trade adjustment. Expenditure switching scales monotonically with flexibility, as theory predicts. Instead, domestic financial variables adjust most, and least monotonically, when exchange-rate variability is highest, suggesting that financial, rather than trade, channels help explain the limits to insulation. Exchange-rate flexibility does provide an effective margin of adjustment to shocks, but reaping the benefits of monetary autonomy enabled by flexibility requires complementary domestic policies to support domestic financial conditions.

title: DP22171 Asset Pricing with Heterogeneous Agents under Limited Information
authors: Riccardo Antonio Cioffi, Samuel Hurtado, Galo Nuño
programme: Monetary Economics and Fluctuations, Asset Pricing
abstract: In this paper, we study the interaction between wealth inequality and asset prices by developing a framework featuring heterogeneous agents, endogenous portfolio choice, and aggregate risk. We solve the model globally under the assumption of limited information: agents forecast prices directly using observable aggregate variables, which makes the problem computationally tractable without sacrificing the economic mechanism. We approximate the drift and volatility of the perceived price process with neural networks and find that the volatility component is highly nonlinear. This endogenously generates time variation in risk premia that local approximation methods cannot produce and that is key to explaining the interaction between inequality and asset returns in our model: through heterogeneous portfolio exposure, aggregate shocks reshape the wealth distribution, which in turn feeds back into asset prices and asset demand through market clearing.

title: DP22170 fereg: Fast high-dimensional fixed-effects regressions in Stata
authors: Johannes Schmieder
abstract: Regressions with many fixed effects are central to applied research, but fitting them to large datasets can be slow. In this article, I present the commands fereg and feppml, which fit linear and Poisson pseudo-maximum-likelihood regressions with high-dimensional fixed effects. Both commands use familiar Stata syntax and pass the computation to a compiled plugin. The plugin chooses among projection, Krylov, and multigrid solvers according to the structure of the fixed effects, checks every result before posting it, and runs on several processor cores. The commands support multiple and interacted fixed effects, group-specific slopes, regression weights, robust and multiway clustered standard errors, saved fixed effects, and prediction. Two simulated examples illustrate their use. In simulated designs with up to ten million observations and default stopping settings, fereg was 6–204 times faster than reghdfe and feppml 11–103 times faster than ppmlhdfe. The commands were also faster than fixest (R) and PyFixest (Python) in all 53 simulated configurations and than the Julia packages FixedEffectModels.jl and GLFixedEffectModels.jl in 52 of 53, with geometric-mean time ratios between 3.0 and 7.7. On administrative data with 1.2 million workers and 117,000 firms, fereg and feppml were at least 3.4 times faster than every other command at every number of cores.

title: DP22168 A Waivable Citizen Veto
authors: Hans Gersbach
abstract: We propose a new democratic institution, the “waivable citizen veto”: citizens can reject a reform, approve it directly, or give elected representatives the final say. We study it in a simple theoretical model. The direct-approval option can be removed without loss to citizens, regardless of their information, if and only if representatives never reject beneficial reforms. We then examine costly investigation that citizens cannot observe. Giving representatives binding authority before they investigate reliably induces investigation whenever delegation offers citizens a better expected outcome than deciding for themselves. Nonbinding advice can achieve the same outcome, but representatives may have no incentive to investigate when citizens disregard their recommendations. The institution thus combines incentives to acquire information with citizens’ initial control over who decides.

title: DP22169 When Institutions Interact: How the Effects of Unemployment Insurance are Shaped by Retirement Policies
authors: Matthew Gudgeon, Pablo Guzman, Johannes Schmieder, Simon Trenkle, Han Ye
abstract: We show that the non-employment effects of unemployment insurance (UI) for older workers depend critically on retirement policy. Using German data, we document large bunching in UI inflows at the age that allows workers to claim their pension following UI expiration. Inflows respond strongly to several UI and pension reforms. We probe the implications of these behavioral responses using a dynamic model and find that Germany's UI and retirement policy changes had substantial effects on the unemployment rate of older workers. Furthermore, we calculate large fiscal externalities from extending UI for older workers, especially under generous retirement policies.

title: DP22160 The Anatomy of Identity
authors: Robert Akerlof
abstract: This chapter develops a conceptual toolkit for understanding how identity shapes economic behavior and social life. Building on Akerlof and Kranton (2000), it examines three aspects of identity, beginning with the pursuit of respect. We first examine how this motivation shapes what people value, the groups with which they identify, and the social equilibria that emerge. We then explore identity prescriptions—expectations about how members of a group ought to behave—and how they arise and persist. Finally, we turn to two motivations that shape how people treat others: anger, which can drive punishment and conflict, and caring, which can be strengthened by identification or weakened by dehumanization. These mechanisms shed light on why studious students may face ridicule, why gender roles persist, why workers sometimes retaliate against managerial discipline, and why feeling looked down upon can fuel populist movements. They also help explain the extraordinary care soldiers show for comrades in battle, as well as the cruelty of schoolyard bullying.

title: DP22165 Money, Power and Civil Society. Reconstructing Pablo Levín’s Interpretation of Marx’s Value-Form
authors: Facundo Alvaredo, Pilar Piqué
abstract: This article reconstructs Pablo Levín’s interpretation of Marx’s derivation of the money-form in chapter 1 of Capital. Marx derives money immanently from the commodity and identifies the simple form of value as the germ of the money-form. Levín argues that this derivation contains a discovery whose theoretical implications Marx did not fully develop: power arises within the elementary commodity relation itself. The polarity between the relative and equivalent forms confers upon the equivalent commodity the power of direct and unconditional exchangeability. The significance of this discovery lies in where it finds power: within a relation whose very premises exclude it. The article shows how this result challenges the modern concept of civil society and its polarity with the modern state. It argues that if power arises immanently within commodity exchange, the defining presupposition of civil society as a sphere devoid of intrinsic power becomes untenable, calling for a reconsideration of the foundations of political economy.

title: DP22166 Elastic in Cash, Inelastic in Repo: Hedge Funds in the Treasury and Repo Markets
authors: Andrea Poinelli, Loriana Pelizzon, Davide Tomio, Benoit Nguyen, Tobias Linzert
abstract: The functioning of sovereign bond markets is closely intertwined with repo markets, where investors finance long positions and source bonds for short sales. We show, theoretically and empirically, how conditions in the cash bond market fundamentally shape repo rates: When demand for cash bonds exceeds available supply, arbitrageurs, notably hedge funds, step in to bridge the gap by shorting bonds and borrowing them in the repo market. These arbitrage strategies drive a wedge between monetary policy rates and repo rates, generating "specialness". To investigate the drivers of investors' demand for repo contracts, we obtain regulatory data covering the entire universe of repos backed by German sovereign bonds. We identify the ultimate borrowers and lenders of securities and estimate their demand and supply elasticities for the repo market. Supply, dominated by the public sector, accounts for 87% of the aggregate elasticity. Demand, driven mainly by hedge funds, is strongly inelastic: a 10% increase in borrowing costs reduces their borrowing by only 1%. Despite being among the most price-elastic investors in cash bond markets, hedge funds are inelastic in repo markets because their bond borrowing bridges the preferred-habitat demand in the cash bond market: their elasticity is inherited from their cash-market counterparties rather than being a primitive. As a result, repo rate specialness emerges as the equilibrium price reflecting demand pressures in the cash bond market, of which collateral scarcity from central bank purchases is a special case. Consequently, the same cash bond market imbalances affect both the pricing of safe assets and repos, two markets that are of crucial importance for the transmission of monetary policy.

title: DP22167 Cross-Border Infrastructure Finance for EMDEs: Patterns, Drivers, and Regulatory Barriers
authors: Stijn Claessens, Daniela Klingebiel, Nicolo Pastrone
programme: Development Economics, Banking and Corporate Finance
abstract: This paper examines whether regulatory barriers, particularly Basel III, constrain commercial banks’ cross-border infrastructure finance (IF) to emerging markets and developing economies (EMDEs). Using IJGlobal deal- and tranche-level data for 2005–2025, we analyse primary financing for new, typically non-recourse project finance (PF) from banks, official-sector lenders, and bond markets. Because country risk may affect bank lending despite Basel III assigning no formal country-risk weights to IF PF, we map borrower countries to the OECD Country Risk Classification (CRC), which aligns with Basel III’s sovereign risk-weight buckets under the Standardised Approach. We compare real, CPI-deflated US-dollar flows across 2005–10, 2011–17, and 2018–25, broadly covering banking crises and early recoveries in EMDEs and advanced economies, Basel III’s design and announcement, and its ongoing implementation. We find that primary PF volumes declined modestly in low-risk countries (CRC 0–2) and more substantially in higher-risk countries (CRC 3–7). Bank participation fell sharply in higher-risk countries, with official-sector lenders substituting for banks. Regressions controlling for key demand and supply factors show a significantly larger decline in PF with bank participation in higher-risk countries as Basel III took effect in lending jurisdictions. The results are economically substantive and statistically robust. However, Basel III was likely only one factor, alongside post-GFC balance-sheet repair, jurisdiction-specific banking stress, and evolving supervisory expectations. Direct tests of specific channels — including the timing of capital, LCR, and NSFR rules, G-SIB designation, and IFRS 9/CECL implementation — show few significant effects. More data and analysis are needed to identify specific supply constraints and systematically document PF risks and returns in EMDEs.

title: DP22161 Age, Education, and Occupational Gradients in Artificial Intelligence Anxiety
authors: Klaus F. Zimmermann, Gokhan Karabulut, Zeynep Keklik, Kıvanç Altıntaş
abstract: Higher levels of anxiety about artificial intelligence (AI) among older and less-educated adults have now been documented in large population-based samples from high-income countries. Much less is known about how these differences arise, whether age and education interact, and whether occupational position helps understand them, particularly in middle-income economies. It evaluates the measurement structure of the scale, tests flexible functional forms and age–education interactions, and decomposes both gradients by occupational skill level, task class, and routine-task intensity. AI anxiety increases approximately linearly with age, whereas its association with education is strongly negative and nonlinear, with the largest gap between the lowest and highest education categories. Age and education largely show additive associations with AI anxiety. The age gradient is weaker among university graduates, although evidence for an interaction is limited for the total score and more evident for several subdimensions. Among the 409 employed respondents, occupational skill level and task class substantially reduce the education gradient but leave the age gradient unchanged: labor-market position helps explain educational but not age differences. Routine-task intensity contributes little beyond broad occupational categories, while professionals and managers report relatively high anxiety conditional on education and task class. Because the cross-sectional design precludes causal and age-period-cohort interpretations, the estimates are conditional associations. Even so, the results show that AI anxiety is not randomly distributed: it is systematically structured by human capital, age, and occupational position in a large middle-income economy.

title: DP22162 US Interest Rate Surprises and Currency Returns
authors: Juan Antolín-Díaz, Gino Cenedese, Shangqi Han, Lucio Sarno
programme: International Macroeconomics and Finance, Asset Pricing
abstract: Currencies that are more exposed to US monetary policy yield positive average excess returns. This result holds for both monetary policy shocks and central bank information shocks that are identified via sign restrictions on intraday changes in interest rates around FOMC announcements. Currency characteristics help explain the heterogeneity of exposures to shocks across currencies and time. We build exposure indices to gauge this effect around policy announcements. Long-short trading strategies that condition on such exposure indices display positive average excess returns, which are especially large on FOMC days and remain significant even after controlling for currency and equity risk factors.

title: DP22163 Do Elite Journals Promote the Production and Diffusion of Breakthrough Ideas? Evidence from Economics
authors: Nagore Iriberri, Marlene Koffi, Ricardo Serrano-Padial
abstract: We study the role of elite journals in the production and diffusion of breakthrough research in economics. Using publications from leading journals between 1985 and 2020, we construct and validate text-based measures identifying breakthrough papers as both novel and influential. We document three facts: top-5 journals’ prioritization of breakthroughs has weakened; the citation premium for breakthroughs has remained stable while that for top-5 publication has risen sharply; and breakthrough research has declined. A simple model highlights the dual role of elite journals: prioritizing breakthroughs encourages their production, but can also reduce innovation by concentrating follow-on research on a few breakthroughs.

title: DP22164 Oligopoly with Mixed Bundling
authors: Volker Nocke, Susumu Sato
abstract: We develop a framework for studying oligopoly with mixed bundling. We consider multinomial logit demand over product combinations and, under this demand system, allow for an arbitrary number of firms and for arbitrary product portfolios, consumer valuations, and marginal costs. Despite the high dimensionality of action spaces and strategic interactions, firms' optimal pricing has a simple structure: each firm optimally sets product prices and bundle discounts to equate the markup it earns from each trade. The primitives governing strategic interaction can be summarized by a type network that captures the value of same-firm purchases, cross-firm purchases, and outside options. We establish the existence and uniqueness of equilibrium. We then apply the framework to study the effects of changes in product costs and qualities, entry, and conglomerate mergers, and show how the welfare effects of mixed bundling depend on market coverage and firm asymmetries.

title: Who Marries Whom? The Role of Segregation by Race and Class
authors: Benjamin Goldman, Jamie Gracie, Sonya R. Porter
abstract: Americans rarely marry outside their race or class group, a pattern with well-documented implications for inequality and intergenerational mobility. Limited exposure may partly explain these low intergroup marriage rates. We instrument for exposure using variation in childhood neighborhoods based on whether other race and class groups had more opposite-sex children of similar age. Exposure increases interclass (high- and low-parent income) marriage but has no detectable effect on interracial (White and Black) marriage. A spatial marriage model predicts that residential segregation—one of many forms of exposure—accounts for more than one-third of marital sorting by class but less than 5 percent by race. (JEL J12, J15, J62, R23)

title: Union Bargaining Power and the Amenity-Wage Trade-Off
authors: Lorenzo Lagos
abstract: This paper studies how collective bargaining affects wages and amenities. By merging collective bargaining agreements (CBAs) to linked employer-employee data in Brazil, I combine rich contracted amenities with wage information. I implement a difference-in-differences strategy that exploits a court ruling enforcing CBA continuation (i.e., ultra-activity) to estimate the effects of union bargaining power. Strengthening unions raises wages and amenities without reducing employment—increasing retention despite some labor-labor substitution. A revealed-preference approach shows that amenities account for 45 percent of total compensation gains. These findings suggest that collective bargaining can offset monopsony power, but employers retain the right-to-manage workforce composition. (JEL J31, J32, J42, J51, J52, O15)

title: Social Push and the Direction of Innovation
authors: Elias Einiö, Josh Feng, Xavier Jaravel
abstract: What are the implications of unequal access to innovation careers for the direction of innovation and inequality? Leveraging novel linked datasets in the United States and Finland, we document that innovators create products more likely to be purchased by consumers like them in terms of gender, socioeconomic status, and age. Homophily exists both within narrow product categories and across industries and has been stable in recent decades. Incorporating this “social push” channel into a growth model, we estimate that unequal access to innovation careers has a large effect on cost of living inequality and long-run growth. (JEL D63, J16, L26, M13, O31, O33, O47)

title: The Causal Effects of Global Supply Chain Disruptions on Macroeconomic Outcomes: Evidence and Theory
authors: Xiwen Bai, Jesús Fernández-Villaverde, Yiliang Li, Francesco Zanetti
abstract: We study the causal effects of global supply chain disruptions by constructing a new index of real-time port congestion using Automatic Identification System data from container ships and a spatial clustering algorithm. We develop a model with search frictions between producers and retailers that links upstream production slack to downstream supply shortages and captures output and price responses to supply chain shocks. The co-movements of output, prices, spare capacity, and market tightness provide novel identification restrictions. We find that demand and supply shocks drove US disinflation in 2020, while the inflation surge in 2021 was driven mainly by supply chain shocks. (JEL C43, E31, F14, F23, L14, L92)

title: Screening and Segmenting: A Consumer Surplus Perspective
authors: Dirk Bergemann, Tibor Heumann, Michael C. Wang
abstract: We analyze consumer surplus when a monopolist can adjust both prices and product qualities across segments, engaging in secondand third-degree price discrimination simultaneously. We characterize the consumer-optimal segmentation and show that it has a striking structure: Consumers with the same value receive the same quality in every segment, though prices differ. Under mild conditions, any segmentation harms consumers if and only if demand is sufficiently more elastic than supply. Hence, potential benefits for consumers depend critically on demand and supply elasticities. These findings have implications for regulatory policy regarding price discrimination and market segmentation. (JEL D42, D83, K21, L12, L15)

title: The Inflation Attention Threshold and Inflation Surges
authors: Oliver Pfäuti
abstract: The recent inflation surge brought inflation back on people's minds. I quantify when and how much attention to inflation changes and derive the macroeconomic implications of these attention changes. I estimate an attention threshold at an inflation rate of 4 percent, that attention doubles when inflation exceeds this threshold, and that supply shocks have stronger and more persistent effects on inflation in times of high attention. Developing a model featuring the attention threshold, I show that attention changes offer a joint explanation for inflation surges, inflation's co-movement with inflation expectations, and a long last mile of disinflation. (JEL D84, E12, E31, E43, E52)

title: Inequality and Racial Backlash: Evidence from the Reconstruction Era and the Freedmen's Bureau
authors: Eric Chyn, Kareem Haggag, Bryan A. Stuart
abstract: How do majority groups respond to narrowing inequality in racially polarized environments? We study this by examining the Freedmen's Bureau, an agency created after the US Civil War to aid former slaves and launch institutional reform in the South. Using new historical records and an event-study approach, we estimate the bureau's impact on political, social, and economic outcomes. Vote shares for Democrats, the party that previously championed slavery and opposed Black civil rights, initially eroded in bureau counties, but these impacts faded as federal oversight weakened. Racial backlash emerged rapidly and persisted, suggesting White majorities sought to offset Black progress. (JEL D63, D72, J15, N31, N41)

title: A Model of the Attention Economy: Data, Platforms, and Discovery
authors: Daniel Chen
abstract: This paper develops a dynamic model of the attention economy featuring two interlinked markets: a product market, where consumers have limited awareness of firms, and an attention market, where platforms attract attention by investing in free services (e.g., social media, streaming, podcasts) and sell targeted ads using data on consumer preferences. The model provides a tractable framework in which platform investment, ad-driven discovery, product demand, and ad revenue are jointly determined. The effects of data and interoperability policies can reverse over time, platform quality may be inefficiently high or low, and the rise of data-rich digital advertising can coincide with a declining ad revenue-to-GDP ratio. (JEL D43, D44, D58, D83, L86, M37)

title: Reproducible Aggregation of Sample-Split Statistics
authors: David M. Ritzwoller, Joseph P. Romano
abstract: Statistical inference is often simplified by sample splitting. This simplification comes at the cost of the introduction of randomness not native to the data. We propose a simple procedure for sequentially aggregating statistics constructed with multiple splits of the same sample. The user specifies a bound and a nominal error rate. If the procedure is implemented twice on the same data, the nominal error rate approximates the chance that the results differ by more than the bound. We illustrate the application of the procedure to several widely applied econometric methods. (JEL C20, C30, C52)

title: Taxing Top Wealth: Migration Responses and Their Aggregate Economic Implications
authors: Katrine Jakobsen, Henrik Kleven, Jonas Kolsrud, Camille Landais, Mathilde Munoz
abstract: Using administrative data from Scandinavian countries, we provide evidence on international migration responses to wealth taxes and evaluate their aggregate economic implications. We find significant migration responses among the wealthy: A 1 percentage point increase in the top wealth tax rate decreases the stock of wealthy taxpayers by about 2 percent. A large fraction of the wealthy are business owners, and their businesses are negatively affected by owner out-migration. The aggregate effects are nevertheless modest: The migration responses to a 1 percentage point increase in the top wealth tax rate reduce employment by 0.02 percent, investments by 0.07 percent, and value added by 0.10 percent. (JEL D31, E22, E24, F22, H24, L26, K34)

title: Front Matter
Durables and the Marginal Propensity to Spend
authors: Nathan Zorzi, Martin Beraja
abstract: Durables represent a large share of households' marginal propensity to spend (MPX). We develop a quantitative model of spending that takes durables into account and matches a rich set of empirical regularities simultaneously. Scaling the response of nondurables provides a poor approximation of the MPX on durables when it comes to its distribution in the population, its persistence over time, and its cyclicality. As an application, we study how the MPX varies with the size of stimulus checks and find that it declines more slowly compared to a model of purely nondurable spending. (JEL D11, E21, E32, E62, G51)

title: Firm Adaptation in Production Networks: Evidence from Extreme Weather Events in Pakistan
authors: Clare Balboni, Johannes Boehm, Mazhar Waseem
abstract: This paper considers how far private adaptation may reduce future vulnerability to climate risks. Using data on monthly firm-to-firm transactions from Pakistan, we find that flood-affected firms are more likely to relocate to safer ground and shift purchases toward suppliers in less flood-prone regions and reached via less flood-prone roads. The results indicate that firms are imperfectly informed about flood risk and update their beliefs following floods. We quantify aggregate impacts using a spatial model of endogenous production network formation. The findings suggest that firms' learning will shape the economic impact of increasingly frequent climate-related disasters. (JEL D22, L14, O13, O14, Q54, R32)

title: The Returns to Government R&D: Evidence from US Appropriations Shocks
authors: Andrew J. Fieldhouse, Karel Mertens
abstract: Based on a narrative classification of all significant postwar changes in R&D appropriations for five major federal agencies, we find that an increase in nondefense R&D appropriations leads to increases in various measures of innovative activity and higher business-sector productivity in the long run. We structurally estimate the production function elasticity of nondefense government R&D capital using the SP-IV methodology of Lewis and Mertens (2024) and obtain implied returns of 140 to 210 percent over the postwar period. The estimates indicate that government-funded R&D accounts for one-fifth of business-sector TFP growth since WWII and imply substantial underfunding of nondefense R&D. (JEL D24, E23, H50, O31, O33, O38)

title: Racial Promotion Gaps
authors: Deepak Hegde, Alexander Ljungqvist, Manav Raj
abstract: We study racial disparities in promotions in a setting in which promotions are formulaic: the US patent office. Using detailed administrative data that allow us to observe who is eligible for promotion when, we document that Black patent examiners experience delays in promotions they are entitled to, slowing their climb to the top of the career ladder by a year and reducing career earnings by 2.5 percent. Institutional features rule out statistical discrimination with accurate priors. Slow promotions even under Black supervisors argue against taste-based animus. Instead, the patterns fit models of belief-based discrimination. (JEL J15, J41, J71, M12, M51, O34)

title: Fighting for Growth: Labor Scarcity and Technological Progress during the British Industrial Revolution
authors: Hans-Joachim Voth, Bruno Caprettini, Alex Trew
abstract: We establish a link between labor scarcity and the adoption of laborsaving technology in industrializing England. During the Napoleonic Wars, more than 10 percent of the male population served in the armed forces. Where recruitment was heavy, more machines economizing on labor were adopted. Naval recruitment, instrumented by warships' coastal access, provides exogenous variation in labor scarcity and suggests that the link between labor shortages and adoption is causal. Where mechanical skills were abundant, the impact of labor scarcity on adoption appears to be larger. (JEL J24, N13, N43, N63, N73, O14, O31)

title: Knowledge Spillovers, Competition, and Individual Careers
authors: Thomas Cornelissen, Christian Dustmann, Uta Schönberg
abstract: Exposure to better peers in the workplace can influence career trajectories through two opposing channels: positively, via knowledge spillovers, and negatively, through competition for advancement. We disentangle these effects by studying untrained labor market entrants and distinguishing between coworkers in the same occupation with whom they are likely to compete versus those with whom they are unlikely to compete. We find robust evidence of persistent knowledge spillovers but also identify countervailing competition effects of comparable magnitude. Both effects are more pronounced for men than for women. (JEL D83, J16, J24, M53, M54, O33)

title: Truth Elicitation in a Nonstrategic Environment
authors: Jacob Glazer, Ariel Rubinstein
abstract: A principal decides which party deserves a prize. Only the parties observe the state that determines who is deserving. The principal gives each party a text describing the conditions under which that party deserves the prize and asks each to report the state. The parties are nonstrategic. Each activates a known cheating procedure whose outcome depends on the state and on the text. Implementation is achieved if, whenever the parties disagree, the liar is identified by the “one-way cheating principle”: The truthful party is the unique party who could not have produced his story had the rival's story been true. (JEL D82, D91)

title: The Unequal Economic Consequences of Carbon Pricing
authors: Diego R. Känzig
abstract: This paper studies the economic impacts of carbon pricing. Exploiting institutional features of the European carbon market and high-frequency data, I identify carbon policy shocks and trace their dynamic effects. A restrictive carbon policy shock raises energy prices, reduces emissions, spurs green innovation, but decreases economic activity—disproportionately burdening poorer households. Not only are the poor more affected because of their higher energy spending, but they also experience larger income losses. These indirect, general equilibrium effects via income and employment play an important role in the transmission of carbon pricing policies, accounting for about two-thirds of the aggregate consumption response. (JEL E23, E24, O44, Q41, Q54, Q55, Q58)

title: Residential Segregation and Unequal Access to Local Public Services in India: Evidence from 1.5 Million Neighborhoods
authors: Sam Asher, Kritarth Jha, Paul Novosad, Anjali Adukia, Brandon Tan
abstract: We study residential segregation and access to public services across 1.5 million urban and rural neighborhoods in India. Muslim and Scheduled Caste segregation in India is high by global standards and only slightly lower than Black-White segregation in the United States. Within cities, public facilities and infrastructure are systematically less available in Muslim and Scheduled Caste neighborhoods. Nearly all regressive allocation is across neighborhoods within cities—at the most informal and least studied form of government. These inequalities are not visible in the aggregate data typically used for research and policy. (JEL H76, J15, O15, O17, O18, R23)
